chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from one of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding the statue/image that is on the carpet, and your eye falls upon it while you are praying, he said: If it has one eye, there is no problem, and if it has two eyes, then (it is disliked/no).

key_terms.عَيْنٍ: Eye (used here to denote the feature of the image)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on praying if a statue with two eyes is on the prayer mat?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'tashbih' (likeness to living beings) as the primary factor in determining the validity of prayer, distinguishing between partial and full representation. It reflects the broader theological concern with idolatry (tawassul to idols) and visual distraction, where the presence of a fully formed image is considered a nullifier or strong dislikeness (makruh) for the worshipper's focus. This ruling underscores the importance of maintaining a pure visual environment during salat to avoid subtle associations with pre-Islamic pagan practices.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from one of his companions,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullahasws, regarding the resemblances which happen to be in the carpet and your eye tends to fall upon it while you are praying Salāt, said: ‘If there was one eye for it, so there is no problem, and if there were two eyes for it, so no’.
en.sarwar: 22. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from certain persons of his people who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about pictures on furnishings which come in one’s view has said, ‘If there is one eye for it, it is not harmful but if it has two eyes then it is not permissible.’”
